title: Final checks: network digital twins, graphs and cloud platform engineering
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Network digital twins (modelling, reachability, path analysis, config verification, snapshots), why graphs fit, and platform-engineering themes for a cloud vendor: multi-tenancy, SDKs, API versioning and reliability.
source: Forward Networks product documentation and datasheets; Oracle Cloud Infrastructure API and SDK docs (opc-retry-token, retries); Google SRE book (SLOs and error budgets); AWS Builders Library (retries, idempotent APIs); networking fundamentals

questions.prompt: What is a network digital twin in the sense of Forward Networks?

options.text: A computed model built from collected device configs and state.
options.why: Right: queries run on the model, with no packets sent into production.

options.text: A second physical network mirroring production hardware port for port in a separate lab.
options.why: That is a lab or staging network, not a software model.

options.text: A packet-capture archive replayed through a simulator for each query that is asked.
options.why: Capture data shows past traffic, not what could happen for any packet.

options.text: A monitoring dashboard that pings every host every minute and plots the latency.
options.why: Probing tests samples of traffic, not all possible behaviour.

questions.explanation: Because the model is derived from configs and state, you can ask "can A reach B and through which hops" or verify a change before deploying.

questions.prompt: A network graph has links A-B, B-C, C-F, A-D, D-E and E-F. What is the number of hops (links) on a shortest path from A to F?
questions.explanation: Both A-B-C-F and A-D-E-F use 3 links, so there are two equal-cost shortest paths (think ECMP). A path-analysis tool must report all of them, not just the first.

questions.prompt: Write Python reachable(graph, src, dst) where graph is a dict mapping a node to a list of neighbours. Return True if dst can be reached from src, using breadth-first search and not looping on cycles.
questions.starter:
from collections import deque

def reachable(graph, src, dst):
questions.explanation: A DFS with an explicit stack also passes. Real network reachability additionally carries a set of packet headers along each edge and applies ACL, NAT and routing constraints at each hop, but the traversal skeleton is the same.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A path query on a digital twin does not need to send any packets into the live network.
questions.reason: The twin is computed from collected configuration and state, so forwarding behaviour can be derived from the model.

whys.a: Correct: the model contains routes, ACLs and topology, so queries are answered by computation.
whys.b: R is the mechanism that makes A true.

questions.explanation: Collection still needs read access to devices and clouds; the twin is only as fresh as its latest snapshot.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Comparing two snapshots of the network shows how its behaviour changed between them.
questions.reason: A graph can store nodes and edges.

whys.a: R is true but generic; it does not explain behavioural diffs.
whys.b: Correct: both true, independent. A snapshot is a point-in-time model; diffing configs and computed paths shows the effect of a change.

questions.explanation: Useful in change review: show what became reachable, what stopped being reachable and which paths shifted.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Verifying an intent such as "production subnets must not reach development subnets" is more complete on a model than by running pings.
questions.reason: A ping from one host tests every possible header, port and path through the network.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because a model can cover all headers and paths, whereas a ping tests one flow. R is false for the same reason.

questions.explanation: Intent checks are assertions over the model, run on every snapshot or proposed change.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Whether host A can reach host B depends only on whether a physical link path exists between them.
questions.reason: Routes, ACLs, NAT and VLAN configuration can all stop traffic along a physically connected path.

whys.d: Correct: A is false and R is true; reachability is a logical property of configuration on top of the physical topology.

questions.explanation: A classic outage cause: the link is up but an ACL or route blocks the flow.

questions.prompt: Match each network-modelling concept to its graph or verification meaning.

right.text: A link, adjacency or forwarding relation
Can A reach B, and hop by hop through which devices
A rule such as "production must not reach development"
A point-in-time copy of collected network state

questions.explanation: Graphs fit because relationships are first-class and most questions are traversals.

questions.text: A network digital twin is built from collected {1} and state, answers path questions through {2} analysis, and uses {3} to compare network behaviour over time.
questions.explanation: Collect, model, query, verify, then compare snapshots over time.

questions.prompt: Why are graph structures a natural fit for network modelling? Select all that apply.

options.text: Links between devices and interfaces are relationships in their own right.
options.why: Right: edges map directly to links and adjacencies.

options.text: Path and reachability questions are traversals that follow edges hop by hop.
options.why: Right: BFS, DFS and shortest paths are standard graph operations.

options.text: A graph removes the need to collect device configuration and state.
options.why: The model is only as good as the collected data.

options.text: A graph guarantees the network configuration is correct.
options.why: A graph represents the network; correctness comes from verifying intent against it.

questions.explanation: Be ready to compare with relational tables: multi-hop paths need recursive joins, which are awkward and slow compared with traversals.

questions.prompt: A service has a 99.9% monthly availability SLO measured by successful requests. In a month with 1,000,000 requests, how many failed requests does the error budget allow?
questions.explanation: 0.1% of 1,000,000 = 1,000. When the budget is spent, teams slow releases and prioritise reliability work.

questions.prompt: A shared API can handle 800 requests per second. It gives each of 8 tenants a rate limit of 120 requests per second. By what percentage is the capacity over-subscribed (sum of limits versus capacity)?
questions.explanation: Sum of limits = 8 x 120 = 960; 960 / 800 = 1.2, so 20% over-subscribed. That can be acceptable because tenants rarely peak together, but it needs load shedding and monitoring.

questions.prompt: Which change to a public REST API most clearly requires a new major version?

options.text: Renaming a response field that existing clients read.
options.why: Right: existing clients would break, so it needs a new version or a deprecation period.

options.text: Adding a new optional field to a response.
options.why: Additive and compatible if clients ignore unknown fields.

options.text: Adding a new endpoint for a new feature.
Adding an optional query parameter with a safe default.
options.why: Backward compatible because old calls behave as before.

questions.explanation: Rules of thumb: additive changes are compatible; removals, renames, type changes and new required inputs are breaking. Publish a deprecation policy and support old versions for a stated period.

questions.prompt: In a shared-schema multi-tenant database, a developer forgets a tenant_id filter in one query and leaks data. What is the best structural defence?

options.text: Enforce scoping below the app, e.g. row-level security.
options.why: Right: make the safe path automatic so one missed WHERE cannot leak.

options.text: Ask developers to remember the filter and add a reminder to the code review checklist for every pull request.
options.why: Relies on human memory, which fails.

options.text: Encrypt the tenant_id column so that other tenants cannot read the values in it.
options.why: Encrypting the id does not stop a query from returning other tenants' rows.

options.text: Give every tenant the same credentials so that queries cannot be mixed up by accident.
options.why: Shared credentials remove isolation rather than adding it.

questions.explanation: Related: per-tenant quotas against noisy neighbours, per-tenant encryption keys, and separate schemas or databases for strict isolation tiers.

questions.prompt: Write Python call_with_retry(send, max_attempts=3). send() returns an object with an integer .status. Return the response unless the status is 429 or at least 500, in which case wait 2**attempt seconds (time.sleep) and try again. After max_attempts raise RuntimeError.
questions.explanation: Real SDKs add jitter, a cap on the delay, respect Retry-After, and only retry idempotent calls or calls carrying an idempotency token.

questions.prompt: True or false: some Oracle Cloud Infrastructure create operations accept an opc-retry-token so a retried request is not executed twice.

options.why: Correct: OCI documents opc-retry-token for safe retries after timeouts or server errors (check each API reference to see which operations support it).
The token exists for exactly this purpose.

questions.explanation: This is the same idea as a payment idempotency key: reuse the token when retrying the same operation.
